root.note: The stone came first, then the colour. The exact road into Ibero-Romance (through Medieval Latin and Old French, or straight from Arabic) is debated.

history: Azul is a colour named after a stone. Persian lāžvard was lapis lazuli, the deep-blue gem, and Arabic made it lāzaward. On the road west the first l was lost, perhaps because it sounded like an article, and Europe was left with azur and azul. English azure is a relative, and lapis lazuli still names the stone. Now look at the walls of Lisbon and Porto. The blue-and-white tiles are azulejos, and almost everyone assumes the name comes from azul. It doesn't. Azulejo comes from Arabic az-zulayj, ‘small polished stone’, and the first tiles were not blue at all. The two words only met on Portuguese walls.
historyEinfach: Azul means ‘blue’. The word comes from Persian. In Persian, it was the name of a deep-blue stone: lapis lazuli. Arabic took the name, and later Europe took it too. Careful: azulejo, the Portuguese tile, looks related to azul. It is not. It comes from an Arabic word for a small, smooth stone.

cognates.note: A tile, from Arabic az-zulayj ‘small polished stone’

elsewhere.text: It looks like ‘a little blue thing’, and many people think so. The Arabic origin says otherwise.
English azure is a cousin of azul, and lapis lazuli is its stone.
